title: Republic Book V: women guardians, the ideal city, and philosophers as kings
summary: Socrates argues that women of the right nature should share the guardians' education and duties, that an ideal state is a standard and not a forecast, and that cities will have no rest from evil until philosophers rule. He separates knowledge of the one true Form from the mere opinion of those who love only fair sights and sounds.

principles.text: Judge differences by whether they bear on the task, not by superficial traits.
principles.quote: When he thinks that he is reasoning he is really disputing, just because he cannot define and divide, and so know that of which he is speaking

principles.text: An ideal is a standard for judging ourselves, so it is not refuted by failing to prove it exists.
principles.quote: Would a painter be any the worse because, after having delineated with consummate art an ideal of a perfectly beautiful man, he was unable to show that any such man could ever have existed?

principles.text: Weigh the beautiful and the ridiculous by the good, not by custom or mockery.
principles.quote: the man was perceived to be a fool who directs the shafts of his ridicule at any other sight but that of folly and vice, or seriously inclines to weigh the beautiful by any other standard but that of the good.

principles.text: Be honest about not knowing: arguing as a mere inquirer risks missing the truth and misleading friends.
principles.quote: to carry on an argument when you are yourself only a hesitating enquirer, which is my condition, is a dangerous and slippery thing

principles.text: Political power and wisdom must be joined for cities to find rest from their evils.
principles.quote: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one

principles.text: Knowing the unchanging reality of a thing differs from holding opinion about its many shifting appearances.
principles.quote: those who see the absolute and eternal and immutable may be said to know, and not to have opinion only
